title: First survey
note: Photographed both street beds. Street Bed 1 still in heavy bloom and badly under-deadheaded. Street Bed 2 mostly finished and full of ripe poppy seed. Two plants unidentified, gladiolus showing possible thrips damage, one stalk with a long vertical split.

title: Questions answered
note: The woolly spikes are snapdragons, no lupines in either street bed. Split stem closed, nothing obvious on the ground. Gladiolus already overwinter in these beds and get lifted and spread each fall, so the corm question is settled: keep the existing routine and add a corm inspection while they are up. Still open: whether the whorled spike plant is veronica or agastache.

title: Inventory rebuilt around what is actually known
note: Seven of nineteen plants are not confirmed, including a large silver-grey mound in Street Bed 2 that has no identification at all, small blue flowers and a round-leaved plant in Street Bed 1, and a question over whether crocosmia is mixed in with the gladiolus. Some plantings were volunteers and are not remembered, so the plan is to photograph properly, check the camera roll from bloom time, stake the unknowns and revisit in spring.

title: Side bed added
note: Narrow raised bed along the house foundation: strawberries still flowering and fruiting, beans on string trellis, sunflowers against the wall, compost tumbler at the end. Sunflowers have clear powdery mildew, almost certainly from still air and a rain shadow next to the wall. Strawberries fruiting in late August means everbearing, so no mowing. Exposure for this bed not yet confirmed. Three of six areas mapped.

title: Site plan drawn from the sketch
note: Hand-drawn map turned into an interactive plan, north at top. Nine areas total, three surveyed. Orientation confirmed as south-up on the original sketch, which settles sun for every bed without asking: Back Bed 2 on the south wall is the hottest and driest spot, the Front Bed on the north wall is the shadiest ground on the property, and the Side Bed faces west, which explains the mildew. The two photographed beds are Street Bed 1 and Street Bed 2.

title: Bed Path surveyed
note: Fourth area. Rosemary, sage, a large stand of shasta daisy gone to seed, bearded iris, a possible euphorbia and a woody volunteer seedling. Mediterranean planting thriving, which is the evidence for full sun and sharp drainage. Key point recorded: this bed must not get the standard fall cut-back, and the iris division window closes in mid-September.

title: Orientation settled for good: north-up
note: Took several rounds. Confirmed three independent ways: the street is the north side, south is where the townhomes are, and the Side Bed Box is on the west wall. All agree on a standard north-up plan, consistent with the original hand sketch and with the street boxes being observed as full sun. Consequences: the two beds between the house and the street are the shadiest ground on the property, not the sunniest; Back Bed 3 on the south wall is compromised by the townhomes; the Side Bed Box is west facing, which explains the mildew; and every genuinely sunny area is out by the street, clear of the house.

title: Driveway Bed 1 surveyed
note: Sunflower patch, zinnias and a wildflower mix. All full-sun plantings, which makes this a fourth sunny area and changes the earlier read that everything sunny was out by the street. Sun recorded as full on the strength of what is planted rather than observed light, with the plants' own vigour as the check. Six of eleven areas surveyed.

title: Replanned around low maintenance and bursty time
note: Goal recorded: a mix of flowers and edibles, but low maintenance is the through-line, and available time varies wildly rather than being steady. Most of the advice given so far was high maintenance, deadheading in particular. Every task now records what happens if it is skipped and is graded as closes, costs or safe. Only seven of thirty-five cannot be made up later. Watering varies by bed and still needs recording per area.

title: Front beds in spring: correction, and the template
note: Photographs from March and April show the front lower and upper beds as the best-looking part of the garden: mass tulips, candytuft, aubrieta, alyssum, primroses and violas, with periwinkle and thyme over the retaining wall. This contradicts the earlier call that they were the shadiest ground and that sun-lovers would disappoint. Two things were missing from the map: the front is terraced, so the beds sit raised and clear of the house shadow, and a north aspect still gets real early and late sun in spring and summer. Reclassified as part sun, spring-lit. More importantly this is the low maintenance model already working on site: bulbs that return plus evergreen mats that cover the ground and need one shear a year.

title: Path Bed: two confirmed
note: Shasta daisy and bearded iris both confirmed by Rachel, moving them off the unidentified list. The iris division window closes in early September, so that task is now the tightest deadline on the board. Shasta division noted as a spring job rather than autumn, since a division going into a wet winter on new roots is the one that rots.

title: Sixth question added: how to get more of it
note: Rachel asked for propagation and renewal to be documented alongside the other five: whether to divide, reseed or buy more, and when. Added to all forty-one plants. Two things fall out of writing it. Autumn division is the wrong call for almost everything here, because new roots going into a wet Seattle winter rot; bearded iris is the exception because it is a surface rhizome. And several plants cannot be divided at all: rosemary and sage go from cuttings taken in late summer, the Japanese maple is grafted so seedlings will not come true, and tulips are honestly a buy-again plant rather than a propagate one.

title: Side bed: pole beans and strawberries confirmed
note: Beans confirmed as pole beans rather than bush, which changes the care: pole beans crop over a long season and depend entirely on frequent picking, where bush beans come all at once. Strawberries confirmed as present; the everbearing versus June-bearing question stays open as a variety note, though late August fruiting makes everbearing very likely.

title: Flower marks added to every plant
note: A small schematic beside each plant name showing the flower form and its real colour. Not photographs: real images cannot be fetched or embedded here, and a form-plus-colour schematic is arguably a better match aid anyway, since form and shade are what you compare against when standing in front of a plant. Sixteen forms cover all forty-one, with a dashed question mark for the ones still unidentified.

title: Upper Bed: six more plants
note: Clematis, bleeding heart, baby's breath, hostas, English daisies and flax all added on Rachel's word. Two more recorded from the spring photographs but not confirmed: forget-me-nots, unmistakable as a blue haze through the bed, and a correction in waiting on the aubrieta, whose big magenta mass has notched petals and needle foliage and reads as creeping phlox instead. Clematis pruning group is unknown and matters more than anything else here, so the instruction for this autumn is to leave it untouched.

title: Upper Bed: dianthus and two more from the photo
note: Dianthus confirmed. Reading further into the spring photograph, two more added as unconfirmed: sweet william, whose dense flat-topped clusters look distinct from the cushion-forming pinks despite both being dianthus, and a wallflower for the orange-bronze mass through the middle. Nineteen plants recorded in this bed and the photograph clearly holds more than that, so it stays open rather than being called complete.

title: Bed names reconciled with the plan
note: Checked every bed name against the Figma labels. All eleven already matched; the drift was on the site plan, which abbreviated them to fit narrow boxes so the map said 'Box 1' where the rest of the page said 'Street Bed Box 1'. The map now wraps and draws the full name, and the validator checks the wrapped text fits rather than checking a hand-written abbreviation.

title: Driveway Bed 2 surveyed
note: Sunflowers, zinnias and gladiolus, and confirmed full sun rather than the morning-sun-likely I had guessed from its position beside the house. Nothing tall stands to its east. That makes the driveway side a second sunny run alongside the street beds, and it moves the gladiolus, zinnia and sunflower jobs onto three beds instead of two. Seven of eleven areas surveyed.

title: Site plan retraced from the Figma proportions
note: Every box re-measured off the Figma plan and scaled rather than approximated, so the relative sizes and positions now match: the street strip with Path Bed at its west end, the two street boxes and the path between them, Driveway Bed 1 across the driveway, and the terracing down the front. Adds the two container outlines from the plan, the planting strip and the property boundary. Back Bed 2 is drawn as its vertical leg only, since it is an L on the plan and a single rectangle covering both arms overlapped the house.

title: Path Bed: herbs out, black-eyed Susans in
note: Sage and rosemary being removed, stump and all, and Rudbeckia going in where they were. Recorded as planned rather than planted. The soil point matters: that corner has grown woody Mediterranean herbs for years and will be lean and dry, which suited them and will not suit rudbeckia, so compost goes in before the plants do. The rosemary layering job is dropped as moot, and the autumn-pruning warning is repointed at the oregano, which is now the woody herb left to protect.

title: Watering recorded per area
note: Front Lower Bed and Upper Bed are on drip line. Side Bed Box, both street boxes, Path Bed and both driveway beds are hose by hand. The three back beds are unconfirmed. Worth noting as an observation rather than a recommendation: the drip is on the two beds that need summer water least, since they are a spring bulb and mat display largely finished by July, while the thirstiest plantings, the dahlias in Street Bed Box 1 and the strawberries and beans in the Side Bed Box, are hose only.

title: Tulips to be lifted from Path Bed
note: Tulip bulbs in Path Bed need moving before the black-eyed Susans go in. Timing is fortunate: tulips are dormant July through October, which is exactly when they can be lifted, so it can happen in the same session as digging out the herbs. Also recorded a connection between two things Rachel told me separately: tulips want a dry summer bake while dormant, and the two front beds where the main tulip display lives are the ones on drip line. If that line runs in July and August it keeps dormant bulbs damp, which is a common reason tulips fade after a year or two instead of returning.

title: Division instructions added
note: Seventeen plants now carry how-and-when division instructions as numbered steps, folded into their card. Video links were searched for rather than recalled, and only three jobs genuinely warrant watching someone do it: bearded iris, dahlia tubers and hostas. The ordinary clump divisions get one written procedure and a link to the university extension guides instead. Three plants are on the list to say they are NOT divided: dianthus dies if you try and goes from cuttings, strawberries renew by runners, and gladiolus is separating cormels rather than dividing anything.

title: Snapdragon rust in Street Bed Box 1
note: Photo is Street Bed Box 1, not Box 2, and the dried spikes are rusted snapdragons with gladiolus behind them rather than spent gladiolus. Rust reverses earlier advice: I had said to cut the spent spikes and leave the plants because snapdragons often overwinter here, which is right for a healthy plant and wrong for a rusted one, since the fungus survives winter on living tissue and debris. They come out roots and all and go in the bin, not the compost. Rust is host-specific to snapdragons, so nothing else in the bed is at risk. Snapdragons also recorded in Box 1 now, not just Box 2.

title: Side Bed Box cleared to strawberries
note: Sunflowers and pole beans both out. The sunflowers are gone from this bed for good: a west wall gave them shade until midday and powdery mildew every year, and the cause was the spot rather than the plant, so the patch stays in the driveway beds. The beans were cut at soil level rather than pulled, leaving the nitrogen nodules in the ground. That makes the side bed a strawberry bed with a run of open ground on it, and the plan for the bed is now written down: thin the mat, peg runners into the cleared ground before the window shuts around mid September, compost on the surface in October with the thickest part against the foundation, and decide by the end of October whether garlic goes in the rest or the strawberries take it over.

title: The side bed settled: strawberries, beans, and the winter gap
note: Decisions taken. The pole beans go back on the string trellis in May, so that strip is fixed as bean ground and nothing perennial goes into it. The strawberry patch spreads forward and along into where the sunflowers stood, from its own pegged runners rather than bought plants. Sunflowers are not coming back to this bed. That leaves one genuinely free slot, and it is a season rather than a corner: October to May, when the strawberries are dormant and the trellis is empty. Garlic or shallots fit it exactly, in in October and out in July, competing with neither crop. Any other summer edible would be fighting the strawberries for the same ground.

title: Next year's side bed planned: four crops and a bag zone
note: The bed is planned through 2027. Strawberries spread into the cleared ground from pegged runners. Pole beans go back on the trellis in May and cucumbers join them on their own strings, on a mildew-resistant variety because this bed proved it is a mildew bed. Garlic takes the October to May window that nothing else wants, so seed garlic gets bought this month before it sells out. Tomatoes stay out of the box entirely and go in fifteen to twenty gallon bags on the concrete, which solves the root depth and, more usefully, keeps the one crop needing daily water from setting the terms for a bed of plants that do not. Checked the three bed crops against each other: they overlap on soil at about pH six to six and a half and agree on the direction of watering, with the cucumber setting the level. The only genuine conflict is feeding, so the cucumber gets fed at its base alone and nothing is ever broadcast over the beans.

title: The box is six inches deep, and that governs the rest
note: Measured at about six inches, set in concrete on every side. That reframes the bed: it is a shallow container rather than a bed cut into ground, and the plan now answers to it. Strawberries turn out to be the right plant rather than the convenient one, because six inches is their natural rooting depth. Garlic will give sound heads rather than big ones. The cucumbers stay in the bed by choice, so they get the technique instead of the depth: one or two plants at most, a sunken pot to water into, mulch, and little and often rather than deep and occasional, which reverses the usual rule because there is no reservoir here to fill. Also corrected a record. The beans' slow start was written down as the shaded-until-midday aspect alone, which made it read as nothing could be done. Six inches of soil under a plant that would root three times that is the other half, and it is the half that watering and feeding can answer.

title: Cucumbers out to a bag, and the bed concentrates on strawberries
note: The box drains, which clears the garlic. The cucumbers move out to a fifteen to twenty gallon bag at the foot of the trellis, which keeps the thing that was actually wanted, a cucumber climbing the strings, while giving it real rooting depth instead of six inches. It also settles a conflict that had no solution inside the box: cucumbers are heavy feeders and beans want nothing, and there was no way to feed one without feeding the other. In a bag there is. That leaves the box holding strawberries, beans and garlic, all of which six inches can carry and none of which need daily attention. The freed ground goes to the strawberry mat rather than to a second berry. Blueberries, raspberries, currants and gooseberries all want more root volume than this box has, and splitting six inches between five crops is how a small bed ends up mediocre at everything. Alpine strawberries are the one berry that would genuinely fit, being shallow rooted, shade tolerant and clump forming, and they would edge the front without needing runner management.
